subject: Post-demo: scaling & SLO playbook (warm pools, burst & streaming)
messages:
From: Jasmine Liu <jasmine.liu@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Morgan <alex@parcelscale.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.ai>, Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwood.ai>
Date: Sun, 9 May 2027 15:10:00 -0700
Subject: Post-demo: scaling & SLO playbook (warm pools, burst & streaming)

Hi Alex — thanks again for the demo time earlier. Quick recap and proposed next steps from our side so we have a clear SLO/scale acceptance criteria for the pilot.

TL;DR proposed targets (please confirm these match ParcelScale expectations):
- Latency: p95 end-to-end (request arrival -> first streaming chunk) <= 150 ms for 256-token streaming responses; p99 <= 400 ms.
- Throughput: sustained 200 req/s for the inference path tied to features A/B.
- Concurrency: support 120 concurrent active sessions (streaming) with acceptable queueing behavior.
- Burst tolerance: tolerate 3x baseline traffic for up to 10 minutes with scale-up path and fallback model variants; cold-to-warm scale-up time target <= 90s.
- Streaming: partial-chunk delivery <= 60ms between chunks, support server-side chunked streaming with early token flush.

Warm pool / autoscale notes:
- Proposal: maintain a warm pool sized for ~40% of steady concurrency (~48 warm slots) to keep KV caches and reduce cache-warm time.
- If warm pool exhausted, we will spin up new nodes; estimated warm node ready-for-streaming window depends on model quantization (see attached CSV hypothesis).
- Queueing policy: small transient queue permitted (<= 2s) for smooth handoffs; enforced backpressure beyond a queue depth threshold (we'll propose exact thresholds).

Requested clarifications from ParcelScale:
1) Is the p95/p99 target above acceptable, or do you need stricter numbers for the pilot?
2) Can ParcelScale tolerate up to ~2s of short queueing for burst absorption, or is zero-queueing required?
3) Are there specific times (calendar windows) when you expect the 3x bursts for testing?
4) Will you be able to share a sample traffic trace (qps over 24h) for realistic benchmarking?

Attachments: initial-scale-hypothesis.csv (CSV) — rough warm-pool sizing and empirical warm-up time estimates we observed in lab.

Proposed next steps:
- ParcelScale confirms targets and provides traffic sample (or we use our synthetic profile).
- Redwood runs a focused benchmark (canary) using your sample traffic + streaming config; target: demonstrate sustained 200 rps and 3x burst handling.
- Draft mutual action plan (MAP) and milestone dates (broad: pilot kickoff, canary run, evaluate SLOs, decide go/no-go).

I'll loop Ben for contractual/credits discussion and Dev for technical runbook. Happy to adjust numbers if your product team has tighter constraints.

Thanks,
Jasmine Liu
Account Executive | Redwood Inference
jasmine.liu@redwood.ai | +1 (415) 555-0192

From: Alex Morgan <alex@parcelscale.com>

Subject: Re: Post-demo: scaling & SLO playbook (warm pools, burst & streaming)

Thanks Jasmine — good write-up. Quick responses inline: 

- p95/p99: p95 <= 150ms is acceptable for our key flows. p99 <= 400ms is OK for the pilot but we'll evaluate tighter constraints later.
- Queueing: we can tolerate brief queueing windows up to ~2 seconds during the burst ramp; anything beyond that starts to meaningfully degrade UX.
- Burst windows: our traffic typically spikes after batch job completions at 11:00 PT and 03:00 PT; we can schedule synthetic spikes outside business hours for the pilot.

I've attached a sample traffic dump from last week (expected-traffic-sample.json).

Two asks from our side: 
1) Please include a short pre-warm strategy in the MAP (what warm pool size you recommend and why).
2) We'd like the MAP to include a canary test plan and pass/fail metrics so Procurement can sign off faster.

If you can get a MAP draft over this week, we can route it internally and allocate 2 engineers for the pilot.

Cheers,
Alex Morgan
VP Engineering | ParcelScale
alex@parcelscale.com

Subject: Re: Post-demo: scaling & SLO playbook (warm pools, burst & streaming)

Jasmine / Ben / Alex — tagging in a few technical clarifications based on your questions and our runtime constraints. Summary and proposed engineering plan below.

1) Warm pool behavior and KV cache:
- Warm pool nodes keep model weights + KV cache primed. For the family of models ParcelScale looked at, KV cache footprint per session is ~1.2MB average; we plan warm-slot sizing assuming worst-case 3MB/session for headroom.
- Warm nodes avoid the full model checkpoint reload path and can accept streaming requests as soon as the dynamic memory subsystems are ready (no additional compile step).

2) Expected warm start times:
- Lab numbers (quantized 4-bit runtime): 55-80s to be ready to emit first streaming chunk.
- If model is non-quantized or has larger vocab embeddings, that can go up to ~120s. We'll include both numbers in the MAP and map to the proposed warm-pool size.

3) Autoscale & burst absorption logic:
- Primary path: route to warm pool until saturated; then spin up new nodes in parallel. We expect the spin-up window above (55-80s) unless the warm pool already covers the bursts.
- Queueing policy: allow transient queueing up to 2s; enforce backpressure beyond 2s with a 429/Retry-After pattern and an optional degraded model variant fallback for critical flows.
- Throttling: suggest a soft rendezvous point of 500ms per upstream slot to smooth spike absorption and avoid thundering herd on warm node allocation.

4) Canary plan (proposed):
- Stage 1: small traffic replay (10% of expected burst) for 30 minutes to validate correctness and missing edge cases.
- Stage 2: progressive ramp to 100% of expected burst over 15 minutes; measure p95/p99, stream chunk intervals, and queue tail latencies.
- Pass criteria: p95 <= 150ms, queueing <= 2s for >=95% of requests during ramp; no service error rate > 0.5%.

Next steps we can own this week:
- Redwood creates a short MAP draft with warm pool recommendation (48 warm slots as Jasmine suggested, plus alternative sizing options), canary test plan, and runbook for 429/backoff + fallback model.
- Run a quick lab benchmark using Alex's traffic sample once received (we'll coordinate timings).

I'll add conservative numbers to the MAP and flag where product tradeoffs exist. Happy to hop on a 30-min technical kick-off with ParcelScale engineers.

Thanks,
Dev Patel
Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
